simple_description: A condition characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks—sudden surges of overwhelming fear and physical distress (racing heart, chest tightness, suffocation) peaking within minutes, often with a fear of dying or having a heart attack.
medical_description: An anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent unexpected panic attacks that are not restricted to particular stimuli or situations. A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or intense discomfort that reaches a peak within a few minutes, during which symptoms such as palpitations, chest pain, choking sensations, dizziness, depersonalization/derealization, and fear of impending doom or dying occur. Followed by persistent concern (>= 1 month) about having further attacks or their consequences.
affected_system: Brainstem autonomic control centers (locus coeruleus noradrenergic hyperactivation, parabrachial nucleus) and limbic fear circuitry (amygdala).
symptoms: Sudden abrupt surge of intense terror reaching a peak within 10 minutes
Pounding heart, racing pulse (tachycardia), or forceful palpitations
Chest pain, tightness, or pressure (frequently mimicking an acute heart attack / angina)
Shortness of breath, feeling smothered, or hyperventilation sensations
Trembling, shaking, sweating, chills, or sudden hot flushes
Dizziness, lightheadedness, unsteadiness, or feeling faint
Feelings of unreality (derealization) or being detached from oneself (depersonalization)
Overwhelming fear of losing control, 'going crazy', or dying on the spot
early_warning_signs: Sudden unprovoked surge of adrenaline and pounding heart in routine situations (driving, shopping, or relaxing at home)
possible_causes: Hypersensitivity of the brainstem 'suffocation false alarm' system (Klein's hypothesis) and hypersensitive central chemoreceptors (CO2 sensitivity)
Abrupt paroxysmal discharge of norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus
Catastrophic cognitive misinterpretation of benign bodily sensations (e.g. interpreting a normal skipped heartbeat as an imminent fatal cardiac arrest)
risk_factors: Female sex (twice as common in women)
Adverse childhood experiences and history of separation anxiety
Heavy smoking, caffeine overuse, or illicit stimulants
disease_types: Panic disorder with agoraphobia (avoidance of places where escape might be difficult, such as crowded markets, buses, or elevators)
clinical_evaluation: Structured psychiatric clinical interview. Essential medical evaluation: 12-lead ECG, cardiac enzymes if high risk, TSH, to safely exclude cardiac ischemia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), or endocrine causes.
diagnostic_tests: 12-Lead Electrocardiogram (ECG) - Critical to rule out cardiac arrhythmias (e.g. Paroxysmal SVT, Wolff-Parkinson-White, Long QT)
Echocardiogram or 24-hour Holter monitoring if palpitations are recurrent
Serum TSH, Free T4, and capillary blood glucose
treatment_overview: Highly treatable condition: First-line psychotherapy is Panic-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT - interoceptive exposure exercises where patients safely experience dizziness and rapid breathing to break catastrophic fears). First-line pharmacotherapy: SSRIs or SNRIs taken daily to prevent future attacks.
medication_classes: First-line Maintenance SSRIs: Sertraline (50-150 mg), Escitalopram (10-20 mg), Fluoxetine
Autonomic blunter for acute physical surges: Propranolol (10-20 mg)
Time-limited acute bridging: Clonazepam / Lorazepam (strictly short-term for 2-3 weeks only while SSRI takes effect)
precautions: DO NOT breathe into a paper bag during hyperventilation (outdated practice that can cause dangerous hypoxia if patient is having asthma or pulmonary embolism instead)
Avoid running to emergency rooms repeatedly once cardiac evaluation has confirmed a structurally normal heart
prevention: Practice slow belly (diaphragmatic) breathing: inhale 4 seconds through nose, hold 4 seconds, exhale 6 seconds through mouth
Cut out energy drinks, strong coffee, and nicotine
complications: Frequent emergency room visits and unnecessary repeated cardiac catheterizations
emergency_signs: First-time chest pain accompanied by radiation to left jaw/arm, diaphoresis, or in patients > 40 with cardiac risk factors (requires emergency 112 / 911 evaluation to rule out acute myocardial infarction before assuming panic attack)

faqs.question: Can a panic attack kill you or stop your heart?
faqs.answer: No. Although a panic attack feels terrifying and like you are having a fatal heart attack or suffocating, the physical surge of adrenaline cannot stop a healthy heart. Attacks peak within 10 minutes and subside as adrenaline naturally breaks down.

hi.name: पैनिक डिसऑर्डर / पैनिक अटैक (Panic Disorder)
hi.summary: अचानक दिल की धड़कन बहुत तेज होना, सीने में भारीपन, सांस फूलना, हाथ-पैर कांपना और ऐसा लगना कि जान जा रही है या हार्ट अटैक आ रहा है, जो 10 मिनट में अपने चरम पर पहुंच जाता है।
hi.advice: गहरी और धीमी सांस लें (पेट से सांस लें)। यह पैनिक अटैक है, हार्ट अटैक नहीं। एक बार ईसीजी कराने के बाद मनोचिकित्सक से सीबीटी और दवा का इलाज करवाएं।

hinglish.name: Panic Attack (Achanak dil tez dhadakna aur maut ka darr)
hinglish.summary: Bina kisi wajah achanak 10 minute me dil ki dhadkan tez hona, paseena aana, saans ghutna aur lagna ki dil ka daura pad gaya.
hinglish.advice: Slow breathing karein, paani piyein aur yaad rakhein panic attack se jaan nahi jaati. Psychiatrist se SSRI medicine lein.

ur.name: پینک ڈس آرڈر (گھبراہٹ کا شدید دورہ)
ur.summary: اچانک دل کا تیز دھڑکنا، سینے میں گھٹن، سانس کا رکنا اور موت کا شدید خوف۔
ur.advice: آہستہ آہستہ گہرے سانس لیں اور ماہر نفسیات سے علاج حاصل کریں۔
